articles.title: Liberia Lifts a Major Barrier to Education
articles.summary:
“Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.  



      


  
  




  
          
                    



                  
          Click to expand Image
          



  
        
  

        
                      
      
        
              Classroom at the KRTTI Demonstration School in Kakata, Margibi County, Liberia. The school has capped enrollment to reduce class size. December 1, 2025.
                    © 2025 Human Rights Watch
          
    


  
Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others said they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.The new policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent said that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.Liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.
articles.content:
“Our children are able to go to school again.” That's how one Liberian parent described the impact of a new government policy banning school registration fees for kindergarten through sixth grade. The policy is already helping families who struggled to pay the fees, removing a longstanding barrier to their children's education.

Click to expand Image Classroom at the KRTTI Demonstration School in Kakata, Margibi County, Liberia. The school has capped enrollment to reduce class size. December 1, 2025. © 2025 Human Rights Watch

Since the policy took effect in September, Liberian child advocates have interviewed parents in four counties to assess whether schools were complying with the ban. The findings offered encouraging early indications: nearly all 20 parents interviewed knew about the policy and had enrolled their children without paying registration fees.

Parents described the difference the policy was making. “The decision by the ministry is so good,” said a parent in Bong County. “It enables our children to go to school free without worry.” Another parent whose children had previously been out of school said, “For some of us that don’t have money, it helps us a lot.”

A Human Rights Watch investigation in late 2025 and early 2026 found that registration fees caused severe hardship for many Liberian families and put education out of reach for others. Some parents told us they had delayed enrolling their children for years because they could not afford the fees. Children described being sent home from school over unpaid fees. Others said they had dropped out of school or turned to child labor.

The new policy has the potential to benefit nearly half a million families, helping children start school on time, stay in school, and avoid child labor. But ensuring that all schools comply will be essential. One parent said that despite the policy, a primary school demanded registration fees for his three children. When he said he couldn't pay, he was told, “No registration, no school.”

The government should monitor and enforce compliance with the fee ban, extend the policy to junior and senior secondary schools, and address other costs—including transportation, uniforms, and textbooks—that keep children from attending school.

Liberia has taken a significant step toward making the right to education a reality for all children, regardless of their financial circumstances. Making education accessible to all children will help reduce inequality and create opportunities for generations to come.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant government policy in Liberia banning school registration fees for K-6, which removes a major financial barrier to education for nearly half a million families. This policy has broad societal impact by enabling children to attend school on time, stay enrolled, and avoid child labor, thus promoting the right to education and reducing inequality. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights early positive outcomes and ongoing challenges, making it a genuinely inspiring development with meaningful real-world benefits.
articles.personality_title: Liberia ends school registration fees for young students, boosting access to education
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – In Liberia, many families struggled to pay school registration fees for children in kindergarten through sixth grade. These fees often stopped children from going to school or caused them to drop out.

**What happened** – Starting in September 2025, the Liberian government banned all registration fees for students from kindergarten to sixth grade. Child advocates interviewed parents in four counties and found that nearly all knew about the new rule and enrolled their children without paying fees.

**Impact** – This policy is helping almost half a million families. Parents say it allows their children to start school on time and stay enrolled without the worry of fees. Some children who had left school or worked instead can now return to class. However, some schools still ask for fees, showing that enforcement is needed.

**What's next step** – The government plans to monitor schools closely to make sure they follow the rule. There are also calls to extend the fee ban to older students in secondary schools and to help with other costs like transportation, uniforms, and books that can stop children from attending school.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Liberia’s ban on school registration fees for young children is opening doors to education for many families, but ongoing efforts are needed to ensure all schools comply and to tackle other costs that keep kids out of class.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le Libéria supprime les frais d'inscription scolaire pour les jeunes élèves, facilitant l'accès à l'éducation
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Au Libéria, de nombreuses familles avaient du mal à payer les frais d'inscription scolaire pour les enfants de la maternelle à la sixième. Ces frais empêchaient souvent les enfants d’aller à l’école ou les faisaient abandonner.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Depuis septembre 2025, le gouvernement libérien a interdit tous les frais d'inscription pour les élèves de la maternelle à la sixième. Des défenseurs des enfants ont interrogé des parents dans quatre comtés et ont constaté que presque tous connaissaient la nouvelle règle et avaient inscrit leurs enfants sans payer.

**Impact** – Cette politique aide près d’un demi-million de familles. Les parents disent que cela permet à leurs enfants de commencer l’école à temps et d’y rester sans souci de frais. Certains enfants qui avaient quitté l’école ou travaillé peuvent maintenant revenir en classe. Cependant, certaines écoles demandent encore des frais, ce qui montre que l’application doit être renforcée.

**Prochaine étape** – Le gouvernement prévoit de surveiller de près les écoles pour s’assurer qu’elles respectent la règle. Il est aussi demandé d’étendre l’interdiction des frais aux élèves plus âgés du secondaire et d’aider pour d’autres coûts comme le transport, les uniformes et les livres, qui empêchent parfois les enfants d’aller à l’école.

**En une phrase** – L’interdiction des frais d’inscription pour les jeunes enfants au Libéria ouvre les portes de l’éducation à de nombreuses familles, mais des efforts restent nécessaires pour que toutes les écoles respectent la règle et pour réduire d’autres coûts scolaires.
articles.personality_title_es: Liberia elimina las cuotas de inscripción escolar para estudiantes jóvenes, mejorando el acceso a la educación
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – En Liberia, muchas familias tenían dificultades para pagar las cuotas de inscripción escolar para niños desde jardín de infancia hasta sexto grado. Estas cuotas a menudo impedían que los niños asistieran a la escuela o provocaban que abandonaran.

**Qué pasó** – A partir de septiembre de 2025, el gobierno liberiano prohibió todas las cuotas de inscripción para estudiantes de jardín de infancia a sexto grado. Defensores de los niños entrevistaron a padres en cuatro condados y encontraron que casi todos conocían la nueva norma y matricularon a sus hijos sin pagar cuotas.

**Impacto** – Esta política está ayudando a casi medio millón de familias. Los padres dicen que permite que sus hijos comiencen la escuela a tiempo y permanezcan inscritos sin preocuparse por las cuotas. Algunos niños que habían dejado la escuela o trabajado ahora pueden regresar a clase. Sin embargo, algunas escuelas todavía exigen cuotas, lo que muestra que se necesita hacer cumplir la norma.

**Próximo paso** – El gobierno planea supervisar de cerca las escuelas para asegurarse de que cumplan con la norma. También se pide extender la prohibición de cuotas a estudiantes mayores en la secundaria y ayudar con otros costos como transporte, uniformes y libros que pueden impedir que los niños asistan a la escuela.

**Resumen en una frase** – La prohibición de cuotas de inscripción para niños pequeños en Liberia está abriendo puertas a la educación para muchas familias, pero se necesitan esfuerzos continuos para que todas las escuelas cumplan y para reducir otros costos que mantienen a los niños fuera del aula.

articles.title: Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms
articles.summary:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Very few Americans have ever eaten foie gras. It’s a niche luxury, served mostly in high-end restaurants, and yet on November 3 it produced some of the most lopsided results of the night in two American cities. In Washington, DC, 73 percent of voters backed a ban on selling […]
The post Animal welfare ballot measures had a strong night in the 2026 midterms first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

Very few Americans have ever eaten foie gras. It’s a niche luxury, served mostly in high-end restaurants, and yet on November 3 it produced some of the most lopsided results of the night in two American cities. In Washington, DC, 73 percent of voters backed a ban on selling the force-fed duck liver, and in Denver, 66 percent did. They weren’t alone. Across this year’s midterms, animal welfare ballot measures had a strong showing, and the pattern in what passed and what didn’t says something about how voters approach animals when the question in front of them is narrow and specific.

Foie gras bans win by wide margins

How foie gras is produced

Foie gras comes from ducks that are force-fed through a metal pipe about 60 times in the final weeks before slaughter, until their livers swell to six to 10 times their natural size. Producers and many fine-dining chefs maintain that the practice is harmless, or at least no worse than other factory farming methods, while veterinary research has concluded it can be quite painful for the birds.

DC and Denver join a growing list

“Tonight DC decided that force-feeding a bird has no place here,” said Cady Witt of Pro-Animal DC, the group that put the measure on the ballot. The District’s ban on sales takes effect in July 2027. California, New York City, Pittsburgh, and Portland, Oregon, already restrict foie gras sales, though the earlier city bans came from officials rather than voters, according to Ballotpedia. Outside the U.S., more than 20 European countries prohibit foie gras production; Brazil banned both its sale and production this year, and India has barred imports since 2014.

Producers and chefs plan to fight back

The votes may not be the last word. A representative from Hudson Valley Farms, the country’s largest foie gras producer, told Axios the company is considering legal challenges. In DC, Bart Hutchins, chef and owner of the restaurant Butterworth’s, wrote in a Washington Post op-ed that he was “incredibly disappointed” the measure reached the ballot, The Hill reported, and he has since hosted four-course foie gras dinners to raise money for a possible lawsuit.

Colorado rejects a constitutional hunting amendment

What Amendment 83 asked voters

Colorado’s Amendment 83 would have written “the right to hunt, fish, and harvest fish and wildlife by traditional methods” into the state constitution and named hunting and fishing as the preferred way to manage wildlife populations. About 55 percent of voters opposed it, according to unofficial results. Supporters argued that hunting and fishing rights shouldn’t depend on statutes or on whoever sits on the state wildlife commission, and 24 states already have some version of the protection in their constitutions. The amendment also exempted nongame and endangered species.

Why “traditional methods” mattered

Hunting and fishing are already protected by Colorado statute, so critics focused on the phrase “traditional methods.” “Read plainly, traditional methods could be interpreted to include practices like poisoning, leg hold traps, gill nets, or baiting and hounding,” Rebecca Niemiec, co-director of Colorado State University’s Animal-Human Policy Center and a Colorado Parks and Wildlife commissioner, told Vox in October. Colorado currently bans those practices. Vox reporter Neel Dhanesha described the stakes for animals that were never the intended target: “Steel-jawed traps and poisons don’t discriminate between, say, a deer, a wolf, and a lynx.” Opponents also worried that naming hunting the preferred management tool could sideline alternatives such as wildlife birth control and relocation.

Where voters drew the line on animal welfare

Conservation funding passes in several states

Wildlife habitat did well this year too. Massachusetts voters approved a measure to fund nature conservation, and voters in Brevard County, Florida, renewed a tax that pays for manatee and dolphin habitat restoration. Conservation measures in Arkansas and Rhode Island also passed.

Broader bans have a harder time

Not every animal measure finds a majority. In 2024, Denver voters turned down a ban on fur sales, which drew 42.4 percent support, and a ban on slaughterhouses within city limits, which drew 36.3 percent, according to Ballotpedia. Set beside this year’s foie gras results, the two votes suggest that measures targeting one specific practice tend to fare better than ones that would reshape a whole industry.

Farm animal laws and the candidates who opposed them

Several candidate races also touched on animal welfare policy. In 2016, Massachusetts voters banned the sale of eggs and pork from hens and pregnant pigs kept in small cages, and California voters passed a nearly identical law two years later. Sen. Roger Marshall of Kansas and Rep. Ashley Hinson of Iowa, both Republicans, have sponsored bills to override those state laws, most recently the Save Our Bacon Act, and both lost their races this year. In Colorado’s Eighth Congressional District, Democrat Manny Rutinel, a state lawmaker and former Earthjustice attorney who sued meat companies over pollution, defeated incumbent Republican Rep. Gabe Evans. In Iowa, Chris Jones, a water quality expert who campaigned on cleaning up livestock and farm pollution, narrowly lost his bid for agriculture secretary. Neither major party has made animal welfare a central campaign issue, but the results will shape how these debates play out in Congress and statehouses over the next two years.

For the campaigners in DC, the win came down to thousands of individual signatures and votes, a slow, ground-level way of changing what a city allows on its menus. Witt closed her statement on election night by thanking the people who did that work: “Thank you to everyone who signed the petition and voted to make DC a kinder place for animals.”

articles.personality_title: Voters in US cities back bans on foie gras and boost animal protection measures
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Foie gras is a luxury food made from the livers of ducks that are force-fed to enlarge their livers. This practice has been controversial because many experts say it causes pain to the birds. Some cities and countries have already banned its sale or production.

**What happened** – On November 3, 2026, voters in Washington, DC, and Denver, Colorado, passed strong bans on selling foie gras, with 73% and 66% support respectively. These cities joined others like New York City and Portland that have similar restrictions. Other animal welfare measures also passed, such as funding for wildlife habitat protection in Massachusetts and Florida. However, Colorado voters rejected a proposal to add hunting rights into the state constitution.

**Impact** – The wide support for banning foie gras sales shows that voters are willing to act against specific animal cruelty practices when given a clear choice. The rejections of broader hunting protections suggest people want careful limits on how wildlife is managed. These votes reflect a growing concern for animal welfare in local laws and show how focused measures can succeed even if broader animal industry changes face challenges.

**What's next step** – The foie gras bans will take effect in 2027, but producers plan to challenge the laws in court. Animal welfare advocates will likely continue pushing for more focused measures that address clear issues. Meanwhile, lawmakers and candidates who opposed animal protection laws faced defeats, signaling that these topics will remain important in future policy debates.

**One-sentence takeaway** – In the 2026 midterms, voters decisively supported banning foie gras sales and other targeted animal protections, showing clear public concern for humane treatment of animals in local policies.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les électeurs de villes américaines soutiennent l’interdiction du foie gras et renforcent la protection animale
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le foie gras est un produit de luxe fabriqué à partir du foie de canards gavés pour le faire grossir. Cette pratique est controversée car de nombreux experts estiment qu’elle cause de la souffrance aux oiseaux. Certaines villes et pays ont déjà interdit sa vente ou sa production.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 3 novembre 2026, les électeurs de Washington, DC, et de Denver, Colorado, ont voté à une large majorité pour interdire la vente de foie gras, avec 73 % et 66 % de soutien respectivement. Ces villes rejoignent d’autres comme New York et Portland qui ont des restrictions similaires. D’autres mesures de protection animale ont également été adoptées, comme le financement de la protection des habitats naturels au Massachusetts et en Floride. En revanche, les électeurs du Colorado ont rejeté une proposition visant à inscrire les droits de chasse dans la constitution de l’État.

**Impact** – Ce fort soutien à l’interdiction du foie gras montre que les électeurs sont prêts à agir contre des pratiques spécifiques de cruauté animale lorsqu’ils ont un choix clair. Le rejet de protections plus larges pour la chasse suggère que les gens souhaitent des limites précises sur la gestion de la faune. Ces votes reflètent une préoccupation croissante pour le bien-être animal dans les lois locales et montrent que des mesures ciblées peuvent réussir même si des changements plus larges dans l’industrie animale rencontrent des obstacles.

**Prochaine étape** – Les interdictions de foie gras entreront en vigueur en 2027, mais les producteurs prévoient de contester ces lois devant les tribunaux. Pendant ce temps, les élus et candidats opposés aux lois de protection animale ont été battus, ce qui indique que ces sujets resteront importants dans les débats politiques à venir.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Lors des élections de mi-mandat de 2026, les électeurs ont clairement soutenu l’interdiction de la vente de foie gras et d’autres protections animales ciblées, montrant une réelle préoccupation pour le traitement humain des animaux dans les politiques locales.
articles.personality_title_es: Los votantes de ciudades estadounidenses apoyan prohibiciones del foie gras y fortalecen medidas de protección animal
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El foie gras es un alimento de lujo hecho con hígados de patos que son alimentados a la fuerza para agrandar sus hígados. Esta práctica es controvertida porque muchos expertos dicen que causa dolor a las aves. Algunas ciudades y países ya han prohibido su venta o producción.

**Qué pasó** – El 3 de noviembre de 2026, los votantes en Washington, DC, y Denver, Colorado, aprobaron con gran mayoría prohibiciones para la venta de foie gras, con un 73% y 66% de apoyo, respectivamente. Estas ciudades se unieron a otras como Nueva York y Portland que tienen restricciones similares. También se aprobaron otras medidas de bienestar animal, como financiamiento para la protección de hábitats en Massachusetts y Florida. Sin embargo, los votantes de Colorado rechazaron una propuesta para incluir derechos de caza en la constitución estatal.

**Impacto** – El fuerte apoyo para prohibir la venta de foie gras muestra que los votantes están dispuestos a actuar contra prácticas específicas de crueldad animal cuando tienen una opción clara. El rechazo a protecciones más amplias para la caza sugiere que la gente quiere límites cuidadosos sobre cómo se maneja la vida silvestre. Estas votaciones reflejan una preocupación creciente por el bienestar animal en las leyes locales y muestran cómo las medidas enfocadas pueden tener éxito incluso si los cambios más amplios enfrentan desafíos.

**Próximo paso** – Las prohibiciones del foie gras entrarán en vigor en 2027, pero los productores planean desafiar las leyes en tribunales. Los defensores del bienestar animal probablemente seguirán impulsando medidas específicas para abordar problemas concretos. Mientras tanto, los legisladores y candidatos que se opusieron a las leyes de protección animal fueron derrotados, señalando que estos temas seguirán siendo importantes en futuros debates políticos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – En las elecciones de medio término de 2026, los votantes apoyaron decisivamente la prohibición de la venta de foie gras y otras protecciones animales específicas, mostrando una clara preocupación pública por el trato humano a los animales en las políticas locales.

articles.title: In win against impunity, Indonesian court orders the reform of Military Justice Law
articles.summary: "Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system."
articles.content:
This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that the 1997 Military Justice Law would be invalid unless amended within two years. The decision was hailed by human rights groups because it means soldiers who commit crimes can be tried in civilian courts.

Article 9 of the Military Justice Law requires active-duty personnel of the Indonesian National Armed Forces to be held accountable exclusively under the military justice system, even when they commit ordinary criminal offenses and human rights violations.

The law was a legacy of the New Order era when the country was under the strongman rule of Suharto, who relied on the military establishment to hold power from 1966 until his resignation in 1998.

The October 15 court ruling was celebrated by human rights groups that have long advocated for the overhaul of the law. They have documented how military courts have failed to investigate and prosecute grave abuses committed by soldiers. They have also expressed concern that military judges are active-duty soldiers, and that judicial investigations and prosecutions often take place within the military chain of command and behind closed doors, with no public oversight.

One of the petitioners asking officials to revoke the law was Eva Meliani Pasaribu, the daughter of Tribrata TV journalist Rico Sempurna Pasaribu, who was killed in June 2024 after reporting about a gambling operation allegedly involving a high-level military official. The military conducted a closed-door investigation and dismissed the allegation for lack of evidence.

Ibnu Syamsu Hidayat, the legal counsel for the petition, addressed the court during the hearing and explained how the law erodes civilian supremacy within a democratic system of governance.

“The dominance of military court jurisdiction over the general judiciary is considered inconsistent with the principles of a constitutional democracy, which mandates that civilian authority must take precedence over military power.”

Hidayat added that the law’s broad provisions have been interpreted to include other criminal offenses committed by soldiers.

“It allows them not only to try military personnel or those equated with them for military crimes and disciplinary violations, but also to adjudicate other criminal cases such as corruption, traffic offenses, domestic violence, narcotics, psychotropics, and child protection cases.”

During the hearing, numerous high-level military officers spoke up in defense of the law. The director general of Defense Forces at the Ministry of Defense, Marshal H. Haris Haryanto, argued that the actions of soldiers, including criminal violations, “can also affect the solidarity and readiness of the military institution.” He added, “Military courts are designed to understand these characteristics so they can deliver decisions that satisfy a sense of justice while also taking into account the interests of national defense.”

The commander of the National Armed Forces, General Agus Subiyanto, said the petition questioning the effectiveness, independence, and accountability of the military justice system “is not based on a comprehensive understanding of the characteristics of military law.”

He emphasized that military judges have the independence of judicial power guaranteed by the constitution and are under the technical judicial supervision of the Supreme Court, adding, “In a military organization, discipline is the primary foundation of national strength. Therefore, the commander’s authority to ensure due process for his subordinates is an inherent legal obligation to maintain operational readiness and the institution’s honor.”

Legal experts who participated in the hearing disagreed, arguing that the law needs reform in order to comply with current human rights standards. Al Araf told the court that the law was drafted under the framework of an “authoritarian political regime” that ignored the principles of rule of law.

“During the New Order era, the legal products enacted in the form of statutes tended to be repressive and merely served as instruments of control for those in power,” he said. “The state enacted laws not within the framework of the rule of law, but solely to fulfill the needs of the rule by law.”

Zainal Arifin Mochtar, another legal expert at the hearing, said the law has to be updated to conform with democratic principles.

“Many issues have emerged, ranging from dual jurisdictions, a lack of synchronization with the spirit of reform, the absence of detailed regulations regarding connectivity, to the issue of independence and accountability of military justice, which is often discussed as a form of legal exceptionalism,” he said.

The move has been widely celebrated by human rights defenders. The Indonesian human rights group KontraS welcomed the court decision, noting that one of its employees has been subjected to an acid attack perpetrated by a group of soldiers. Under the new ruling, soldiers could be tried in public courts in such cases.

“This ruling closes a legal loophole that has long been perceived as protecting individual soldiers from accountable law enforcement, while also marking a new chapter in upholding the rule of law and fulfilling the mandate of security sector reform in Indonesia,” read their statement.

The reform is the result of decades of work and activism, as explained by Human Rights Watch (HRW).

“Justice for civilian victims of military abuses shouldn’t be blocked by an unfair military court system,” read their statement. “Amending the law on military justice will support efforts begun decades ago to ensure the Indonesian military is a professional, credible institution whose soldiers are held accountable when they commit serious abuses.”

Free Press Unlimited said the court ruling is a victory against impunity.

“The Constitutional Court’s eagerly awaited ruling is a true victory for justice and a critical step for Indonesia in its fight against impunity,” read their statement on the ruling. “We urge lawmakers to act promptly and adhere to this landmark ruling as soon as possible. Only then can Indonesia finally turn a corner and ensure that cases involving military personnel will be dealt with by civilian courts, as it should be.”

Both Indonesian and international civil society groups are urging lawmakers to start the reform process by consulting the public and various stakeholders. Activists argue that public vigilance has to be sustained, especially since Indonesia’s current president, Prabowo Subianto, is a former general dismissed from the military for committing human rights violations. Since coming to power in 2024, he has expanded the military’s role in civilian governance.
articles.reasoning: The Indonesian Constitutional Court ruling mandates reform of a military justice law that previously shielded soldiers from civilian prosecution, addressing decades of impunity and human rights abuses. This decision has broad societal significance as it strengthens civilian oversight, accountability, and the rule of law in Indonesia, with detailed context on the law, its historical background, and the impact on victims and society.
articles.personality_title: Indonesian court orders reform of military justice law to end impunity
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Indonesia has a law from 1997 that lets soldiers accused of crimes be tried only in military courts. This law has made it hard for civilians to get justice when soldiers commit abuses. The law was created during a time when the military had a lot of control over the country.

**What happened** – On October 15, 2026, Indonesia’s Constitutional Court ruled that this military justice law must be changed within two years or it will become invalid. The court said soldiers who commit crimes should be tried in civilian courts, not just military ones. This decision came after a long fight by human rights groups and families of victims.

**Impact** – This ruling is important because military courts often fail to fairly investigate or punish soldiers who break the law. Military judges are also soldiers, which can lead to unfair trials. Now, soldiers accused of crimes like corruption, violence, or abuse may face civilian courts, which are more independent. This change could help victims get real justice and make the military more responsible.

**What's next step** – Lawmakers in Indonesia need to rewrite the military justice law soon to meet the court’s demands. articles.personality_title_fr: La cour indonésienne ordonne la réforme de la justice militaire pour mettre fin à l'impunité
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – En Indonésie, une loi de 1997 permettait aux soldats accusés de crimes d’être jugés uniquement par des tribunaux militaires. Cette loi empêchait souvent les civils d’obtenir justice lorsque des soldats commettaient des abus. Elle a été créée à une époque où l’armée avait beaucoup de pouvoir dans le pays.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 15 octobre 2026, la Cour constitutionnelle d’Indonésie a décidé que cette loi sur la justice militaire devait être modifiée dans les deux ans, sinon elle deviendrait invalide. La cour a déclaré que les soldats coupables de crimes devaient être jugés par des tribunaux civils, pas seulement militaires. Cette décision fait suite à une longue lutte des groupes de défense des droits humains et des familles des victimes.

**Impact** – Cette décision est importante car les tribunaux militaires ne parvenaient souvent pas à enquêter ou punir équitablement les soldats fautifs. Les juges militaires sont aussi des soldats, ce qui peut compromettre l’impartialité des procès. Dorénavant, les soldats accusés de crimes comme la corruption, la violence ou les abus pourraient être jugés par des tribunaux civils, plus indépendants. Cela pourrait aider les victimes à obtenir une vraie justice et rendre l’armée plus responsable.

**Prochaine étape** – Les législateurs indonésiens doivent rapidement réécrire la loi sur la justice militaire pour respecter la décision de la cour. Les militants souhaitent que le public participe à ce processus afin que la nouvelle loi protège les droits humains. Beaucoup surveillent cette réforme, surtout que le président actuel a un passé militaire controversé.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – La décision de la cour indonésienne impose de réformer la justice militaire, permettant aux tribunaux civils de rendre les soldats responsables et d’améliorer la justice pour les victimes.

articles.title: ‘Peace begins in our hearts’: Children close Muscat forum with a message to the world
articles.summary: Children from across the world sent a message of peace from the Omani capital Muscat on Monday, calling for an end to hatred, respect for diversity and the protection of human rights.
articles.content:
Their message closed the two-day Muscat Plan of Action Forum, held on the International Day for Tolerance, marked by the UN every 16 November.

“Peace begins in our hearts, and in our belief that we all belong to one humanity,” the children said, describing understanding as the bridge between peoples and coexistence as the foundation for a safe and prosperous future.

They pledged to build bridges of solidarity, stand up for children’s rights, protect the planet and act as ambassadors for peace in their own communities.

On the forum’s second day, UN officials, religious and traditional leaders and experts discussed how to turn the goals of the Muscat Plan of Action – launched at UN Headquarters in New York in June – into practical programmes and partnerships.

Difference is not the problem

Mohamed bin Said bin Khalfan Al Mamari, Oman’s Minister of Endowments and Religious Affairs, said the plan aims to strengthen the role of religious and traditional leaders and Indigenous Peoples in preventing conflict and combating hate speech.

“Difference in itself does not create conflict, just as similarity does not guarantee peace,” said Mr. Al Mamari.

Peace “is not merely the absence of violence or the cessation of conflicts and wars,” he continued, but needs a system built on justice, trust and security.

The minister called for stronger local mediators, a better link between early warning and institutional response and a bigger role for women and young people.

Words before violence

Chaloka Beyani, the UN Special Adviser on the Prevention of Genocide, said tolerance is the basis for peace, human rights and coexistence, warning that discrimination and exclusion can escalate into incitement to violence and crimes against humanity.

UN News/Abdelmonem Makki

He pointed to the 1994 Genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda and the 1995 Srebrenica genocide as examples of where rhetoric fuelling marginalization and hatred can lead.

“Hate speech and intolerance feed each other in a vicious circle,” said Mr. Beyani, urging action at an early stage, before words turn into hostility or violence.

Metropolitan Emmanuel of Chalcedon, of the Ecumenical Patriarchate of Constantinople, warned that atrocity crimes can be preceded by years of rhetoric that strips people of their identity and casts them as a threat.

Imams, priests, rabbis and community leaders can spot tensions early and confront inflammatory speech, he said.

Egypt’s Minister of Endowments, Osama Al-Azhari, called for an “acquaintance of civilizations” in place of conflict, citing the Quranic verse: “And We made you into peoples and tribes that you may know each other.”

Settling disputes the traditional way

Queen Gladys Mbuya of Cameroon, a lawyer and human rights defender, described how a traditional leader resolved a dispute between Indigenous Bororo herders and farmers whose crops were being destroyed by livestock.

After a full-day meeting at his palace, both sides agreed that the herds would be kept off cultivated land and the farmers would put up fences.

Traditional mediation looks for solutions acceptable to everyone, rather than simply punishing the party at fault, said Queen Mbuya.

Five-year roadmap

The forum closed with the presentation of a global framework for putting the Muscat Plan into practice between 2027 and 2032.

articles.personality_title_fr: Des enfants et des dirigeants unis à Mascate pour promouvoir la paix et la tolérance
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Chaque année, le 16 novembre, les Nations Unies célèbrent la Journée internationale de la tolérance pour encourager le respect et la compréhension entre les peuples. **Ce qui s'est passé** – Pendant deux jours, des enfants du monde entier ont partagé un message demandant la paix, le respect de la diversité et la protection des droits humains. Ils ont dit que la paix commence dans nos cœurs et ont promis de travailler pour la paix dans leurs communautés. Pendant ce temps, des dirigeants ont discuté de la manière de transformer les objectifs du Plan d'action de Mascate — lancé plus tôt à l'ONU à New York — en programmes concrets pour arrêter les discours de haine et prévenir les conflits.

articles.personality_title_es: Niños y líderes se unen en Mascate para promover la paz y la tolerancia
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Cada año, el 16 de noviembre, las Naciones Unidas celebran el Día Internacional de la Tolerancia para fomentar el respeto y la comprensión entre las personas. Este año, un foro llamado Plan de Acción de Mascate se llevó a cabo en Mascate, Omán, reuniendo a niños, líderes religiosos y expertos para hablar sobre la paz y el fin del odio.

**Qué pasó** – Durante dos días, niños de todo el mundo enviaron un mensaje pidiendo paz, respeto a la diversidad y protección de los derechos humanos. Dijeron que la paz comienza en nuestros corazones y prometieron trabajar por la paz en sus comunidades. Mientras tanto, líderes discutieron cómo convertir los objetivos del Plan de Acción de Mascate—lanzado antes en la ONU en Nueva York—en programas reales para detener el discurso de odio y prevenir conflictos.

**Impacto** – El foro mostró que la paz es más que solo detener la violencia; requiere justicia, confianza y seguridad. Los líderes destacaron que las diferencias entre las personas no causan conflictos por sí solas, y que actuar temprano para detener el discurso de odio puede prevenir violencia grave, como el genocidio. Líderes tradicionales compartieron cómo resuelven disputas buscando soluciones justas para todos, no solo castigando a una parte.

**Próximo paso** – Se presentó un plan de cinco años, de 2027 a 2032, para poner en práctica el Plan de Mascate en todo el mundo. Este plan se centra en construir alianzas, involucrar a las comunidades locales y apoyar a líderes que puedan detectar y detener el odio temprano. También fomenta un mayor papel para mujeres y jóvenes en los esfuerzos de paz.

**Mensaje en una frase** – Niños y líderes mundiales en Mascate unieron fuerzas para promover la paz mediante la comprensión, la acción temprana contra el odio y métodos tradicionales de resolución de conflictos respaldados por una nueva hoja de ruta de cinco años.
